industry.usGenerics: The US is the largest generics market and the hardest. Three wholesaler-led buying groups buy most generics, so prices fall every year on old products (mid-single digits is the industry norm) and a new generic loses most of its price within months once several rivals enter. Money is made on volume, on cost (backward-integrated APIs) and on products that few can copy: injectables, controlled substances, inhalers, complex topicals. Plant compliance is the gate: a warning letter or OAI stops new approvals from a site.
industry.tariffs: On 2-Apr-2026 the US imposed a 100% Section 232 tariff on patented medicines; generics and their ingredients were exempted 'at this time' (effective 31-Jul-2026 for listed firms, 29-Sep-2026 for others). On 21-Jul-2026 President Trump said imported generics would stay tariff-free for about two years, then face 100% from Aug-2028 and 200% from 2029 unless makers build US plants (a social-media post, not yet law). About 90% of India's pharma exports to the US are generics (GTRI, Sep-2026).
industry.tariffsSrc: EY Tax News (2-Apr-2026); Covington (Apr-2026); PharmExec (22-Jul-2026); Business Standard (29-Sep-2026)
industry.europe: European generics are bought through national tenders and price-controlled pharmacy markets: low prices but stable volumes and few US-style collapses. Scale, a broad portfolio and reliable supply win; Aurobindo is among the top ten generic companies in eight European countries and passed EUR1bn of sales in FY26 after a decade of acquisitions (Actavis, Generis, Apotex).
industry.growthMarkets: Growth Markets (Canada, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, China, India and others) are smaller, branded or semi-branded and grow faster; Aurobindo entered India's branded market only in 2022 (Veritaz) and added GLS and the Khandelwal brands.
industry.arv: ARV formulations are anti-HIV medicines sold mostly through donor-funded tenders (PEPFAR, Global Fund); volumes are large, prices are set by tender and margins thin; donor funding cuts are a risk.
industry.api: India still imports most penicillin intermediates from China. The government's PLI scheme pays Rs240 cr per 10,000 t of Pen-G produced, and from 29-Jan-2026 a one-year minimum import price applies to Pen-G (Rs2,216/kg), amoxicillin (Rs2,733/kg) and 6-APA (Rs3,405/kg).
industry.apiSrc: DGFT notification 56/2025-26 (29-Jan-2026) via TaxGuru, Medical Dialogues; Q3FY26 call
industry.biosimilars: Biosimilars (copies of biologic drugs) need large plants and clinical trials (~US$450mn invested by Aurobindo since 2018). Europe buys oncology biosimilars through tenders with 10+ players per molecule and 75-85% price erosion (CEO); regulators in Europe and the US are starting to waive phase-3 efficacy studies, which lowers the entry cost for everyone.

critiques: Underlying US growth is weak: US revenue in dollars fell 7% in FY26 and Q1FY27's $399mn is below Q1FY25's $426mn; FY27 growth comes from the rupee (~10% weaker) and Lannett
Injectables are stuck: two Eugia sites under warning letters and a third (Unit III) re-classified OAI; management now guides single-digit growth
Returns have not followed the capex: ROE between 7.5% and 11.4% in FY22-26 against a ~12% cost of equity, after Rs3,000 cr+ of capex a year (Pen-G, China, biologics)
Working capital is heavy: inventory 326 days (Screener, FY26), so earnings convert to cash slowly
Governance discount: 7% of equity pledged by promoters; electoral bonds bought days after a promoter director's ED arrest (2022); legacy land-allotment cases
The bull case is cheapness: ~18x FY28E EPS vs pharma peers at 25-80x trailing; Lannett, Pen-G, China and biosimilars give several earnings levers
Tariff tail risk: a 100% US tariff on imported generics from 2028 would hit the most US-exposed Indian generics maker hardest, partly offset by its US plants
